gap: No result ChatGPT got states that a typical submersible well pump runs on 230 V single-phase. Such a pump can only be powered by a source with a 120/240 V outlet, such as the L14-30R on a mid-size gas generator or the L14-30 on Anker's F3800 Plus. A plain 120 V power station does not have one, and even a 1/2 hp pump needs a source rated about 2 kW, because pump makers size generators to hold the voltage dip at startup to 35% or less.
standout_why: ChatGPT ran no searches and got no results, so there were no rival pages to read. I compared against its answer instead. That answer says generators suit 'heavy appliances' and power stations suit 'electronics, short outages', but it never mentions output voltage (120 V vs 120/240 V), the L14-30 outlet, or the startup sizing that well pumps require. Those are the electrical facts that decide whether a home-backup plan works at all.
decides: For home backup with a 230 V well pump or other 240 V loads, the plan only works with a source that has a 120/240 V L14-30 outlet. That can be a gas or dual-fuel generator (Champion 201077: 6,500 W running, 8,125 W starting, L14-30R) or a 240 V-capable power station (Anker SOLIX F3800 Plus: 120V/240V on NEMA L14-30R, up to 6,000 W), not a compact 1 kWh, 1,800 W 120 V unit. For 120 V-only loads (router, fridge, laptops) the choice stays open, and a power station works if its continuous and surge ratings exceed the load's.

findings.label: Typical residential submersible well pump supply voltage
findings.value: 230 VAC single-phase, 3-wire, ±10% tolerance, 6 A (1/2 hp model 5FR05P4-3W230)
findings.note: Maker's product page. Franklin also sells 115 V versions (e.g. 96210530, 5FR05P4-3W115) in the same collection. Those appeared only in search results and I did not open them, so whether a given home's pump is 230 V must be checked on the pump label. The page lists no locked-rotor or starting amps.

findings.label: Minimum generator size to start a submersible pump motor
findings.value: 1/2 hp: 2.0 kW externally regulated / 1.5 kW internally regulated; 3/4 hp: 3.0 / 2.0 kW; 1 hp: 4.0 / 2.5 kW; 1.5 hp: 5.0 / 3.0 kW
findings.source_title: Grundfos SP Installation and Operating Instructions, 10.2 Guide for engine-driven generators in submersible pump applications (p. 33)
findings.note: Grundfos's own words: 'The table is based on typical +176 °F (+80 °C) rise continuous duty generators with 35 % maximum voltage dip during startup'. For kVA ratings, multiply by 1.25. I read this through a ManualsLib copy, and the values came from a flattened table, so check them against the printed page. The table is for engine-driven generators. I found no pump-maker figure for battery inverters.

findings.label: AC output voltage and 240 V outlet
findings.value: 120V/240V dual-voltage; NEMA L14-30R 120V/240V~ 25 A max, 6,000 W max; 120V~ 20 A outlets 2,400 W max; 1x NEMA TT-30 3,000 W 120 V
findings.source_title: Anker SOLIX F3800 Plus product page
findings.note: The page also says 'Add Plus, then directly connect to your Transfer Switch'. It gives no surge rating and never uses the phrase 'split phase'. It showed 'Sold Out' and 'Price Loading', so I have no price.

findings.label: Output and 240 V outlet
findings.value: Gasoline 8,125 W starting / 6,500 W running; propane 7,325 W starting / 5,850 W running; 120/240V 30A locking outlet (L14-30R) plus 2x 120V 20A 5-20R duplex
findings.note: Maker's page. It shows no price, only 'Find Local'.

findings.label: Output, UPS switchover, price
findings.value: 1,800 W output (2,700 W 'Lifting Power'), 1,024 Wh LiFePO4, 10 ms UPS switchover; $499.00
findings.source_title: BLUETTI Elite 100 V2 Portable Power Station | 1,800W 1,024Wh
findings.note: Price read with storecheck.py from BLUETTI's US Shopify store. The product text gives no AC voltage and no motor-surge figure.
